title: Ion Solvation Theory
section: Part I: Derivation of the Average Solvation Number
text:
Part I: Derivation of the Average Solvation Number
Motivation. Solvation free energy reflects the cost of surrounding a charged species with a shell of oriented solvent molecules — specifically, the entropy decrease due to free solvent molecules binding to ions and limiting accessible configurations. We follow a thermodynamic route to relate the average solvation number and binding equilibria to chemical potentials and activity coefficients, naturally bridging molecular-scale solvation with macroscopic observables.


Step 1: Foundational Definitions and Mass Balances

The Average Solvation Number
We define the average solvation number (number of bound solvent molecules per cation) as:
\[
\bar{h} = \frac{\text{total bound solvent molecules}}{\text{total cations}}
        = \frac{n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^b}{n_C^t}
\]
where \(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^b\) is the total number of bound water molecules and \(n_C^t\) is the total number of cations.


Mass Balance of Species
Define:

\(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^t\): total water molecules

\(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^f\): free (unbound) water molecules

\(n_{C_i}\): cations with \(i\) bound water molecules

\(N\): maximum solvation sites per cation

From mass balance:
\[
n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^t = n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^f + \sum_{i=0}^N i\, n_{C_i}
\qquad
n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}^b = \sum_{i=0}^N i\, n_{C_i}
\qquad
n_C^t = \sum_{i=0}^N n_{C_i}
\]
Thus:
\[
\bar{h} = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^N i\, n_{C_i}}{\sum_{i=0}^N n_{C_i}}
        = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^N i\, x_i}{\sum_{i=0}^N x_i}
\]
where \(x_i = n_{C_i}/n_C^t\) is the mole fraction of cations with \(i\) bound water molecules.




Step 2: Microscopic and Macroscopic Equilibria

Distinguishing Equilibrium Constants (\(k\) vs \(K\))
It is crucial to distinguish between the macroscopic constant \(K_i\), which describes the overall formation of a species with \(i\) bound molecules, and the microscopic constant \(k\), which describes the intrinsic affinity for any single specific binding site. Macroscopic constants are influenced by combinatorics; the microscopic constant is not.
The macroscopic equilibrium constant \(K_1\) relates to all species with one bound solvent molecule regardless of which site is occupied:
\[
K_1 = \frac{[C_1]}{[C_0][\mathrm{H_2O}]}
\]
In contrast, microscopic constants \(k_i\) refer to binding at specific individual sites. The macroscopic constants relate to populations summed over indistinguishable microstates, while microscopic constants describe specific binding site interactions.


Combinatorics of Binding Sites
For cations with \(N\) identical binding sites and \(i\) bound waters, the number of unique microstates is:
\[
\Omega_{N,i} = \binom{N}{i} = \frac{N!}{i!(N-i)!}
\]
For model simplicity, we assume all sites bind identically, so \(k_i = k_j\), though \(K_i \neq K_j\) due to combinatorics.




Step 3: Deriving a Closed-Form Expression for \(\bar{h}\)
Define equilibrium constants based on activities. In general:
\[
K_i = \frac{a_i}{a_{i-1}\, a_w} \implies a_i = a_0\, a_w^i \prod_{j=1}^i K_j
\]
Assuming \(a_i \approx x_i\):
\[
x_i = x_0\, x_w^i \prod_{j=1}^i K_j
\]

Relating Macroscopic and Microscopic Constants
For the general equilibrium \(C_{i-1} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons C_i\), normalizing concentrations by the number of corresponding microstates:
\[
k = \frac{\left(\frac{[C_i]}{\Omega_{N,i}}\right)}
        {\left(\frac{[C_{i-1}]}{\Omega_{N,i-1}}\right)[\mathrm{H_2O}]}
\implies
K_i = \frac{\Omega_{N,i}}{\Omega_{N,i-1}}\, k
\]
Using the binomial forms:
\[
\frac{\Omega_{N,i}}{\Omega_{N,i-1}}
= \frac{N-i+1}{i}
\implies
\boxed{K_i = \frac{N-i+1}{i}\, k}
\]


Deriving the Mole Fractions
\[
\prod_{j=1}^i K_j = \prod_{j=1}^i \frac{N-j+1}{j}\cdot k^i
= \binom{N}{i} k^i
\]
Therefore:
\[
x_i = x_0\,(k x_w)^i \binom{N}{i}
\]
Substituting into the solvation number:
\[
\bar{h} = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^N i\, x_0 (kx_w)^i \binom{N}{i}}
               {\sum_{i=0}^N x_0 (kx_w)^i \binom{N}{i}}
        = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^N i\,(kx_w)^i \binom{N}{i}}
               {\sum_{i=0}^N (kx_w)^i \binom{N}{i}}
\]


Evaluating the Binomial Sums
Recall the binomial identity and its derivative with respect to \(x\), multiplied by \(x\):
\[
\sum_{i=0}^N \binom{N}{i} x^i = (1+x)^N
\qquad
\sum_{i=0}^N i\binom{N}{i} x^i = Nx(1+x)^{N-1}
\]
Let \(y = kx_w\):
\[
\bar{h} = \frac{Ny(1+y)^{N-1}}{(1+y)^N} = \frac{Ny}{1+y}
\]
Substituting back:
\[
\boxed{\bar{h} = \frac{N k x_w}{1 + k x_w}}
\]
This compact expression links the average number of bound solvent molecules per cation to the microscopic binding constant \(k\), the number of solvation sites \(N\), and the free water mole fraction \(x_w\).

title: Ion Solvation Theory
section: Part II: Derivation of the Solvation Activity Coefficient
text:
Part II: Derivation of the Solvation Activity Coefficient
Motivation. Having established a molecular model for \(\bar{h}\), the next step is to quantify its thermodynamic effect. Binding of solvent molecules depletes the free solvent available for mixing, altering the chemical potential of all species. This section connects the microscopic solvation model to macroscopic activity coefficients.


Step 4: Connecting Solvation to Gibbs Free Energy
Assume complete dissociation \(E \to \nu_C C + \nu_A A\). The chemical potential of the electrolyte is:
\[
\mu_E = \nu_C \mu_C + \nu_A \mu_A
\]
The total Gibbs free energy is \(G = n_0\mu_0 + n_C\mu_C + n_A\mu_A\), and the excess Gibbs energy is:
\[
G^E = G - G^{\mathrm{ideal}}
\implies
\frac{G^E}{RT} = n_0 \ln\gamma_0^{\mathrm{slv}}
               + n_C \ln\gamma_C^{\mathrm{slv}}
               + n_A \ln\gamma_A^{\mathrm{slv}}
\]
The chemical equilibrium condition requires:
\[
\mu_{ci} = \mu_{c0} + i\mu_0^f
\]
Applying mass balances reduces the chemical Gibbs energy to \(G^{\mathrm{chem}} = n_0\mu_0^f + n_C\mu_{c0} + n_A\mu_{a0}\), showing by comparison that \(\mu_0^f = \mu_0\), \(\mu_{c0} = \mu_C\), \(\mu_{a0} = \mu_A\).

Defining Activity Coefficients from Chemical Potential
For the solvent, equating the free and apparent chemical potentials gives:
\[
\boxed{\ln\gamma_0^{\mathrm{slv}} = \ln\!\left(\frac{x_0^{\mathrm{slv}}}{x_0}\right) = \ln\alpha_0}
\]
For the cation, using the infinite dilution normalization \(\gamma_C^{\mathrm{slv}} \to 1\) as \(x_C \to 0\):
\[
\boxed{\ln\gamma_C^{\mathrm{slv}} = \ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i^\infty}\right)}
\]




Step 5: Solvent Depletion and Alpha Corrections

Solvent Correction Factor \(\alpha_0\)
\[
\alpha_0 = \frac{x_w^{\mathrm{slv}}}{x_w}
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
x_w^{\mathrm{slv}} = \frac{n_w - \sum_i \bar{h}_i n_i}{n_w + \sum_i n_i(1-\bar{h}_i)}
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{\alpha_0 = \gamma_0^{\mathrm{slv}} =
\frac{1 - \sum_i \bar{h}_i\, \dfrac{n_i}{n_w}}
     {x_w + \sum_i x_i(1 - \bar{h}_i)}}
\]


Solute Correction Factor \(\alpha_i\)
Using \(n_i^{\mathrm{slv}} = n_0(1+kx_w)^N\) and rearranging:
\[
\alpha_i = \frac{n_t}{n_t^{\mathrm{slv}}}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+kx_w)^N}
\qquad
\alpha_i^\infty = \lim_{x_w\to 1}\alpha_i = \frac{1}{(1+k)^N}
\]


Final Expression for Solvating Species (Cations)
\[
\boxed{\gamma_i = \frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i^\infty} =
\frac{(1+k_i)^{N_i}}{x_w\,(1+k_i x_w)^{N_i}
\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n_w}\displaystyle\sum_j n_j(1-\bar{h}_j)\right)}}
\]


Final Expression for Non-Solvating Species (Anions, \(k_i = 0\))
\[
\boxed{\gamma_i = \frac{1}{x_w\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n_w}\displaystyle\sum_j n_j(1-\bar{h}_j)\right)}}
\]
Interpretation: Even though the anion does not bind water directly, its activity coefficient still reflects the global scarcity of free water — arising from competition by hydrated cations reducing available solvent for entropy of mixing. In the dilute limit \(x_w \to 1\), \(n_j \to 0\), this recovers \(\gamma_i \to 1\) as expected.

title: Ion Solvation Theory
text:
Summary

Key Assumptions

Selective solvation — cations solvate; anions have \(k = 0\)
Identical independent sites — all \(N\) sites on a cation bind with the same microscopic constant \(k\)
Activity–concentration equivalence — \(a_i \approx x_i\) in the equilibrium expressions



Final Expressions







Quantity
Expression




Average solvation number \(\bar{h}_i\)
\(\dfrac{N_i k_i x_w}{1 + k_i x_w}\)


Solvent activity coefficient \(\gamma_0\)
\(\dfrac{1 - \sum_i \bar{h}_i n_i/n_w}{x_w + \sum_i x_i(1-\bar{h}_i)}\)


Cation activity coefficient \(\gamma_i\)
\(\dfrac{(1+k_i)^{N_i}}{x_w(1+k_i x_w)^{N_i}(1+\sum_j \frac{n_j}{n_w}(1-\bar{h}_j))}\)


Anion activity coefficient \(\gamma_i\)
\(\dfrac{1}{x_w(1+\sum_j \frac{n_j}{n_w}(1-\bar{h}_j))}\)





Alpha Correction Factors
\[
\alpha_0 = \frac{x_w^{\mathrm{slv}}}{x_w}
\qquad
\alpha_i = \frac{n_t}{n_t^{\mathrm{slv}}}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+k_i x_w)^{N_i}}
\qquad
\alpha_i^\infty = \frac{1}{(1+k_i)^{N_i}}
\]
The non-ideal solvation contribution to the chemical potential is directly related to these:
\[
\frac{G^E_{\mathrm{slv}}}{RT} = n_0\ln\alpha_0 + \sum_{i\neq 0} n_i\ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i^\infty}\right)
\]

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
section: Part 1: Entropy Production and the Derivation of Driving Forces
text:
Part 1: Entropy Production and the Derivation of Driving Forces
We follow the development in Molecular Theory of Gases and Liquids (Hirschfelder, Curtiss, Bird) and Multicomponent Diffusion (Curtiss, Bird), assuming the reader is comfortable with the standard continuum balance laws and basic thermodynamics. Transport in a given direction is a spontaneous microscopic process that dissipates free energy and produces entropy; under local equilibrium, the macroscopic dynamics can be described by thermodynamic forces and their conjugate fluxes.

The Fundamental Entropy Balance
Goal: State the general entropy balance and determine the entropy production \(\sigma\).
We start from the local entropy balance in divergence form:
\[
\rho\frac{D\hat{S}}{Dt} = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{s} + g_S
\tag{1}\]
where \(\mathbf{s}\) is the entropy flux and \(g_S \ge 0\) is the local entropy production. Here \(D/Dt\) is the substantial derivative:
\[
\frac{D(\cdot)}{Dt} = \frac{\partial(\cdot)}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla(\cdot)
\]
We combine (i) a Gibbs relation for a multicomponent mixture with (ii) the conservation laws. Starting from the equilibrium Gibbs relation per unit mass:
\[
d\hat{U} = T\,d\hat{S} - p\,d\hat{V} + \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mu_i}{M_i}\,d\omega_i
\tag{2}\]
Taking the substantial derivative and rearranging:
\[
T \frac{D\hat{S}}{Dt}
= \frac{D\hat{U}}{Dt}
+ p\,\frac{D(1/\rho)}{Dt}
- \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mu_i}{M_i}\,\frac{D\omega_i}{Dt}
\tag{3}\]


Step 1.1: Substitute Conservation Laws
We replace the derivatives using the conservation equations.
A. Conservation of energy (MTGL Eq. 11.1-4):
\[
\rho\frac{D\hat{U}}{Dt}
= -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}
- p\,(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})
- (\boldsymbol{\tau}:\nabla\mathbf{v})
+ \sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\mathbf{g}_i
\tag{4}\]
B. Continuity equation (MTGL Eq. 11.1-2):
\[
\frac{D(1/\rho)}{Dt}
= -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{D\rho}{Dt}
= \frac{1}{\rho}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})
\tag{5}\]
C. Species continuity (MTGL Eq. 11.1-1), neglecting reactions (\(r_i = 0\)):
\[
\rho\frac{D\omega_i}{Dt} = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}_i
\tag{6}\]


Step 1.2: The Substitution
Multiply Equation 3 by \(\rho\) and substitute Equation 4–Equation 6. The \(p(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})\) terms cancel, giving:
\[
\rho\frac{D\hat{S}}{Dt}
= -\frac{1}{T}\nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}
-\frac{1}{T}(\boldsymbol{\tau}:\nabla\mathbf{v})
+ \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\mathbf{g}_i
+ \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}_i
\tag{7}\]


Step 1.3: Isolate Divergences
Using \(\nabla\cdot(A\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla A + A\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{x}\):
\[
-\frac{1}{T}\nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}
= -\nabla\cdot\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}}{T}\right) - \frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}
\]
\[
\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}_i
= \nabla\cdot\!\left(\frac{\mu_i\mathbf{j}_i}{M_i T}\right) - \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
\]
Substituting back gives the entropy balance in the form Equation 1, with the entropy production:
\[
\boxed{
g_S
= -\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}
-\frac{1}{T}(\boldsymbol{\tau}:\nabla\mathbf{v})
- \sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
+ \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mathbf{j}_i\cdot\mathbf{g}_i}{T}
}
\tag{8}\]



Connection to Phenomenological (Flux–Force) Laws
Thermodynamics requires \(g_S \ge 0\). To guarantee positivity, one postulates linear phenomenological laws: each flux is proportional to its corresponding thermodynamic driving force.

General Structure: Flux \(\times\) Force
From Equation 8, the entropy production is a sum of products:
\[
g_S
= \underbrace{-\frac{1}{T^2}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T)}_{\text{thermal}}
\underbrace{-\frac{1}{T}(\boldsymbol{\tau}:\nabla\mathbf{v})}_{\text{viscous}}
\underbrace{-\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\left[\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right) - \frac{\mathbf{g}_i}{T}\right]}_{\text{diffusive}}
\tag{9}\]
Written abstractly as \(\sigma = \sum_k \mathbf{J}_k\cdot\mathbf{X}_k \ge 0\), where \(\mathbf{J}_k\) is a flux and \(\mathbf{X}_k\) its conjugate thermodynamic force.


Identifying the Thermodynamic Forces
Heat conduction. Using \(\nabla(1/T) = -\nabla T/T^2\):
\[
-\frac{1}{T^2}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T) = \mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)
\]
Flux–force pair: \(\mathbf{J}_q = \mathbf{q}\), \(\mathbf{X}_q = \nabla(1/T)\). Temperature gradients produce entropy through heat conduction.
Viscous dissipation. \(\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{visc} = \boldsymbol{\tau}\), \(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{visc} = -(1/T)\nabla\mathbf{v}\). Velocity gradients produce entropy.
Diffusion. The diffusive flux–force pair is \(\mathbf{J}_i = \mathbf{j}_i\) and:
\[
\mathbf{X}_i = -\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right) + \frac{\mathbf{g}_i}{T}
\]
Chemical-potential gradients and body forces produce entropy through mass transfer.


Summary of Flux–Force Pairs








Phenomenon
Flux \(\mathbf{J}\)
Force \(\mathbf{X}\)




Heat conduction
\(\mathbf{q}\)
\(\nabla(1/T)\)


Viscous dissipation
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}\)
\(-(1/T)\nabla\mathbf{v}\)


Diffusion (species \(i\))
\(\mathbf{j}_i\)
\(-\nabla(\mu_i/M_i T) + \mathbf{g}_i/T\)





Onsager Relations and Cross-Effects
To ensure \(g_S \ge 0\), assume linear flux–force relations:
\[
\mathbf{J}_a = \sum_b L_{ab}\,\mathbf{X}_b
\tag{10}\]
with a positive-semidefinite coefficient matrix \(\mathbf{L}\). Off-diagonal terms capture the Soret effect (temperature gradient driving mass flux) and the Dufour effect (mass flux driving heat flux).

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
section: Part 2: Defining the Generalized Driving Force
text:
Part 2: Defining the Generalized Driving Force
Goal: Transform the raw chemical-potential gradient into the force-density form used by Crothers, Delacourt, and Weber.
The diffusive entropy production is:
\[
g_S^{\mathrm{diff}}
= - \sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\left[\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right) - \frac{\mathbf{g}_i}{T}\right]
\tag{11}\]
Since \(\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i = \mathbf{0}\), there are only \(v-1\) independent diffusive mass fluxes. The conjugate thermodynamic driving forces are similarly constrained by the Gibbs–Duhem equation.

Step 2.1: Deriving the Curtiss–Bird Driving Force \(d_i\)
We start from the Gibbs–Duhem equation in the entropy representation:
\[
U\,d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + V\,d\!\left(\frac{p}{T}\right) - \sum_{i=1}^v N_i\,d\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) = 0
\tag{12}\]
Step 2.1a: Divide by volume. Divide by \(V\) and define \(u := U/V\), \(c_i := N_i/V\):
\[
u\,d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + d\!\left(\frac{p}{T}\right) - \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,d\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) = 0
\]
Step 2.1b: Replace differentials by spatial gradients (local equilibrium):
\[
u\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \nabla\!\left(\frac{p}{T}\right) - \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) = \mathbf{0}
\]
Expanding the pressure term using the product rule:
\[
\nabla\!\left(\frac{p}{T}\right) = \frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p + p\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)
\]
Substituting:
\[
(u+p)\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p - \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) = \mathbf{0}
\tag{13}\]
Step 2.1c: Replace \((u+p)\) by enthalpy density. Since \(h = u+p = \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\bar{H}_i\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) - \frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p - \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\bar{H}_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) = \mathbf{0}
\]
Step 2.1d: Convert \(\nabla(1/T)\) to \(\nabla T\). Using \(\nabla(1/T) = -\nabla T/T^2\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{T}\right) - \frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p + \sum_{i=1}^v c_i\,\frac{\bar{H}_i}{T^2}\,\nabla T = \mathbf{0}
\tag{14}\]
Step 2.1e: Replace \(c_i = \rho_i/M_i\) (Curtiss–Bird Eq. 1.4):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v \rho_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right) - \frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p + \sum_{i=1}^v \rho_i\,\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T = \mathbf{0}
\tag{15}\]
Step 2.1f: Decouple heat and mass transfer contributions.
Since \(\sum_i \rho_i/\rho = 1\), we write Equation 15 term-by-term:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v \left[
\rho_i\,\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
- \frac{\rho_i}{\rho}\,\frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p
+ \rho_i\,\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T
\right] = \mathbf{0}
\tag{16}\]
Ignoring viscous dissipation and adding the pressure and enthalpy terms inside the species summation so the Gibbs–Duhem constraint can be invoked:
\[
g_S
= -\frac{1}{T^2}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T)
- \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mathbf{j}_i}{\rho_i}\cdot\Bigg[
\underbrace{\rho_i\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
- \frac{\rho_i}{\rho}\,\frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p
+ \rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T}_{\text{(A) constrained by Gibbs--Duhem} = 0}
\;\underbrace{-\rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T}_{\text{(B) ``free'' term}}
+ \rho_i \frac{\mathbf{g}_i}{T}
+ \frac{1}{T}\frac{\rho_i}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v\rho_j\mathbf{g}_j\Bigg]
\tag{17}\]
Term (A) equals zero by the Gibbs–Duhem constraint Equation 16. The last two body-force terms also cancel (see Supplementary Material):
\[
g_S
= -\frac{1}{T^2}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\nabla T)
- \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mathbf{j}_i}{\rho_i}\cdot
\left[
-\rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T
\right]
\]
Heat-flux decomposition and cancellation of the enthalpy term.
Define the modified heat flux (Curtiss–Bird):
\[
\mathbf{q}^{(h)} := \mathbf{q} - \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i}\,\mathbf{j}_i
\tag{18}\]
Substituting \(\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}^{(h)} + \sum_i (\bar{H}_i/M_i)\mathbf{j}_i\) into the thermal contribution, the enthalpy terms cancel exactly, and we recover the full entropy production with the modified heat flux:
\[
g_S
= -\frac{1}{T^2}(\mathbf{q}^{(h)}\cdot\nabla T)
- \sum_{i=1}^v \frac{\mathbf{j}_i}{\rho_i}\cdot\Bigg[
\rho_i\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
- \frac{\rho_i}{\rho}\,\frac{1}{T}\,\nabla p
+ \rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i T^2}\,\nabla T
+ \rho_i\,\frac{\mathbf{g}_i}{T}
+ \frac{1}{T}\,\frac{\rho_i}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v \rho_j\mathbf{g}_j\Bigg]
\]
Step 2.1g: Define the generalized driving force \(d_i\).
Focus on the diffusion entropy production. Following Curtiss–Bird, introduce driving forces \(d_i\) (units: reciprocal length) via the normalization \((cRT/\rho_i)d_i\):
\[
\boxed{
\frac{cRT}{\rho_i} d_i
= T\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
+ \frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i}\nabla\ln T
- \frac{1}{\rho}\nabla p
- \mathbf{g}_i
+ \frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v \rho_j\mathbf{g}_j
}
\tag{19}\]


Step 2.2: Convert to Force-Density Units
Define \(\mathbf{F}_i := cRT\,d_i\), so multiplying Equation 19 by \(\rho_i\):
\[
\mathbf{F}_i
= \rho_i T\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
+ \rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i}\nabla\ln T
- \omega_i\nabla p
- \rho_i\mathbf{g}_i
+ \omega_i\sum_{j=1}^v \rho_j\mathbf{g}_j
\tag{20}\]
Step 2.2a: Substitute mass-to-molar relations. Use \(\rho_i = c_i M_i\) and \(g_i = X_i/M_i\) (where \(X_i\) is force per mole).
Step 2.2b: Evaluate each term:
\[
\rho_i T\nabla\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{M_i T}\right)
= c_i\!\left(\nabla\mu_i - \frac{\mu_i}{T}\nabla T\right)
\]
\[
\rho_i\frac{\bar{H}_i}{M_i}\nabla\ln T
= c_i\,\frac{\bar{H}_i}{T}\,\nabla T
\]
Step 2.2c: Assemble and factor:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{F}_i
= c_i\!\left(\nabla\mu_i + \frac{\bar{H}_i-\mu_i}{T}\,\nabla T
- \frac{M_i}{\rho}\nabla p
- X_i
+ \frac{M_i}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v c_j X_j\right)
}
\tag{21}\]

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
section: Part 3: From Driving Force to the Curtiss–Bird Flux Law
text:
Part 3: From Driving Force to the Curtiss–Bird Flux Law
Goal: Apply Onsager’s phenomenological framework to obtain the Curtiss–Bird constitutive flux equation.

Step 3.1: Write the Dissipation Function
Multiply the entropy production by \(T\) to form the dissipation function \(\Phi := Tg_S\). Substituting the definition of \(d_i\):
\[
\Phi = -\mathbf{q}^{(h)}\cdot\nabla\ln T \;-\; \sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\frac{cRT}{\rho_i}\,d_i
\tag{22}\]
Define shorthand forces:
\[
L_0 := \nabla\ln T,\qquad L_i := \frac{cRT}{\rho_i}\,d_i
\]


Step 3.2: Count the Independent Flux–Force Pairs
Flux side. \(\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i = \mathbf{0}\) leaves \(v-1\) independent diffusion fluxes.
Force side. \(\sum_{i=1}^v \rho_i\,d_i = 0\) by Gibbs–Duhem, leaving \(v-1\) independent forces.
Removing redundancy. Since \(\sum_i \mathbf{j}_i = \mathbf{0}\), we may subtract any species-independent vector from each \(L_i\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot L_i
= \sum_{i\neq k} \mathbf{j}_i\cdot (L_i - L_k)
\]


Step 3.3: Apply Onsager Linear Phenomenological Laws
\[
\mathbf{q}^{(h)} = -R_{00}\,L_0 - \sum_{j\neq k} R_{0j}\,(L_j - L_k)
\tag{23}\]
\[
\mathbf{j}_i = -R_{i0}\,L_0 - \sum_{j\neq k} R_{ij}\,(L_j - L_k),\qquad i\neq k
\tag{24}\]
with Onsager reciprocal relations \(R_{ij} = R_{ji}\).
Physical meaning of off-diagonal terms:



Coefficient
Effect




\(R_{00}\)
Thermal conduction


\(R_{ii}\)
Self-diffusion


\(R_{i0} = R_{0i}\)
Soret effect (thermal → mass flux)


\(R_{0j} = R_{j0}\)
Dufour effect (mass → heat flux)


\(R_{ij},\; i\neq j\)
Cross-diffusion





Step 3.4: Extend the Summation to All Species
Summing Equation 24 over all \(i\neq k\) and requiring \(\sum_{i\neq k}\mathbf{j}_i = -\mathbf{j}_k\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v R_{ij} = 0 \qquad \text{for all } j
\]
This defines \(R_{kj} := -\sum_{i\neq k} R_{ij}\), allowing the sum to extend to all species:
\[
\sum_{j\neq k} R_{ij}(L_j - L_k)
= \sum_{j=1}^v R_{ij}L_j
\]
Result:
\[
\mathbf{j}_i = -R_{i0}\,\nabla\ln T \;-\; \sum_{j=1}^v R_{ij}\,\frac{cRT}{\rho_j}\,d_j,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,v
\tag{25}\]


Step 3.5: Identify Physical Transport Coefficients
Thermal diffusion coefficient:
\[
D_i^T := R_{i0} \qquad [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}]
\]
With \(\sum_i D_i^T = 0\) (only \(v-1\) independent).
Symmetric multicomponent diffusivity:
\[
\tilde{D}_{ij} := \frac{cRT\,R_{ij}}{\rho_i\rho_j} \qquad [\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}]
\]
Onsager symmetry gives \(\tilde{D}_{ij} = \tilde{D}_{ji}\) immediately.


Step 3.6: The Curtiss–Bird Constitutive Flux Equation
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{j}_i = -D_i^T\,\nabla\ln T \;-\; \rho_i\!\sum_{j=1}^v \tilde{D}_{ij}\,d_j
}
\tag{26}\]
Reading this equation:

First term \((-D_i^T\,\nabla\ln T)\): the Soret (thermal diffusion) contribution. A temperature gradient alone drives a mass flux even at uniform composition.
Second term \((-\rho_i\sum_j \tilde{D}_{ij}\,d_j)\): the multicomponent diffusion contribution. The flux of species \(i\) depends on the driving forces of all species \(j\) through the symmetric matrix \(\tilde{D}_{ij}\).

Connection to Newman’s equation 13.1. The combination that emerges from substituting Equation 26 into the Stefan–Maxwell force balance is:
\[
A_j^i := \frac{D_j^T}{\rho_j} - \frac{D_i^T}{\rho_i}
\]
which is precisely the quantity Newman defines. This confirms that Newman’s thermal diffusion correction is not an independent ingredient — it is the Stefan–Maxwell re-expression of the Curtiss–Bird Soret coefficient.

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
text:
Summary
Equation 21 provides a generalized view of multicomponent diffusion driving forces: gradients in chemical potential, temperature (Soret effect), pressure (pressure diffusion), and differential body forces that act differently on different species (forced diffusion). In electrochemical applications, none of these terms can always be neglected. Examples include:

Thermogalvanic cells (temperature gradients)
Pressure-driven transport in PEM fuel cells
Sedimentation in semi-solid flow batteries
Centrifugal isotope separation

The “Newman approach” incorporates the electrostatic potential into the chemical potential to define the electrochemical potential, \(\bar{\mu}_i = \mu_i + z_i F\phi\), so the driving force becomes \(\nabla\bar{\mu}_i = \nabla\mu_i + z_iF\nabla\phi\). This is consistent with the generalized derivation above. More rigorous electrodynamic treatments (Fong and Mandadapu) recover this familiar form explicitly from first principles via the internal entropy production.

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
text:
Connection to Stefan–Maxwell Framework
Under isothermal, isobaric conditions with no body forces, the Curtiss–Bird driving force leads naturally to the Stefan–Maxwell equations:
\[
c_i \nabla \mu_i
= \sum_{j\neq i} K_{ij}\left(\mathbf{v}_j-\mathbf{v}_i\right)
\tag{27}\]
This is a force balance: the thermodynamic force on species \(i\) (left) is balanced by frictional forces between species \(i\) and each other species. The Stefan–Maxwell coefficients relate to binary diffusivities as:
\[
K_{ij} = \frac{RT\,c_i c_j}{c_T D_{ij}}
\]
Fuller and Newman show this can be inverted to obtain the Onsager flux form:
\[
N_i = -\sum_k \left(L_{ik}\,c_i c_k\,\nabla \mu_k\right)
\]
These equivalences — driving-force form, Stefan–Maxwell, Onsager flux — will serve as the starting point for examining what assumptions allow reduction to Ohm’s law, Fick’s laws, and the Nernst–Planck equation.

title: Origin of Driving Forces from Fundamentals
section: Supplementary Material: The Body Force Terms
text:
Supplementary Material: The Body Force Terms
In Equation 17 we introduced a body-force term and stated it contributes zero. Here we show why explicitly.
The diffusive fluxes satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i = \mathbf{0}\), so for any species-independent vector field \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{\Psi}
= \boldsymbol{\Psi}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i = 0
\]
Define the mixture-average body force:
\[
\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}} := \sum_{j=1}^v \frac{\rho_j}{\rho}\,\mathbf{g}_j
\]
Decompose \(\mathbf{g}_i\):
\[
\mathbf{g}_i = \big(\mathbf{g}_i-\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}}\big) + \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}}
\]
Substituting into the body-force entropy production:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\frac{1}{T}\mathbf{g}_i
= \sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i\cdot\frac{1}{T}(\mathbf{g}_i-\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}})
+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{T}\,\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^v \mathbf{j}_i}_{=\; 0}
\]
Physical interpretation. A body force that accelerates all species equally (\(\mathbf{g}_i = \mathbf{g}\) for all \(i\)) produces \(\mathbf{g}_i - \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}} = \mathbf{0}\) and drives no diffusion. Only differential body forces (e.g., electric forces depending on charge, magnetic forces) contribute to the driving force — which is the physically correct result.
Expanding:
\[
\mathbf{g}_i - \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}}
= \mathbf{g}_i - \frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v \rho_j\mathbf{g}_j
\]
This replacement of \(\mathbf{g}_i\) by \(\mathbf{g}_i - \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{mix}}\) inside the driving term produces the additional mixture-average correction:
\[
-\mathbf{g}_i
\;\longrightarrow\;
-\mathbf{g}_i + \frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{j=1}^v \rho_j\mathbf{g}_j
\]
which is precisely the “extra” term appearing in Equation 19.
